Case study

CarePath

A calmer way to move through a public hospital visit.

A navigation layer for public services. It starts with what a person is trying to do — see a doctor, get a certificate, chase a pension — and turns that into one clear step at a time, right up to the official government system, then hands over.

The problem

The service usually exists.
Finding it doesn't feel like it does.

Most public-service frustration isn't the transaction itself — it's everything around it: which office handles this, what to bring, whether you're on the right step, and what happens after you submit.

  • People know the outcome they want, rarely the government service name for it.
  • Official portals ask for department-level decisions before intent is even clear.
  • Once you're "in" a process, there's no reliable way to tell where you stand.
  • Low connectivity, older phones and partial translations quietly exclude people.
How might we build a simple, trustworthy layer that moves people through a public-service journey step by step — without pretending to replace the government system underneath it?

Approach

What I was actually designing

1

Start with the outcome

Users pick what they're trying to do, not a department. "I need to see a doctor," not "OPD registration."

2

One step, always visible

Every journey has exactly one current step, a progress position, and one obvious next action — never a wall of options.

3

Stay alongside the system, not on top of it

CarePath explains and prepares. The official service — ORS, in this prototype — stays the source of truth for the actual transaction.

4

Design for the phone that's actually in someone's hand

Accessibility controls, read-aloud, language switching and a low-connectivity path are load-bearing, not an afterthought bolted on at the end.

5

No control lies about being interactive

If it looks tappable, it does something — advances a step, opens the real destination, or clearly says why it's disabled.

Process — 10 days

Frame, then build outward

This was a solo sprint, built end to end in ten days. I front-loaded the pattern that everything else would reuse, then spent the back half making sure nothing in the interface was decorative.

Day 1–2

Frame the service problem

Defined CarePath as guidance, not a replacement portal. Chose to start every flow from outcomes, not department structure.

Day 3–4

Build the reusable journey pattern

Service selection → step → official handoff → reference. Every later journey is this pattern, restated.

Day 5–7

Expand into four services

Healthcare (built furthest), pension, certificates and grievances, each carrying the same skeleton with different content.

Day 8

Design for access

Accessibility panel, language switching, read-aloud, and a keypad-friendly concept for people without a smartphone.

Day 9

Make every interaction real

Went screen by screen removing dead-end buttons and cards that looked interactive but weren't.

Day 10

Test the whole loop

Ran all four journeys end to end, switched languages both directions, checked back/exit/restart, verified official links.

Walkthrough

Healthcare, the deepest journey

Healthcare is the fully working part of the prototype — booking guidance, a live visit tracker, and the staff side that actually drives it. Four moments from that journey:

01 — Starting from intent

What do you need today?

No department names. Five plain-language entry points, and a standing reminder that CarePath isn't the hospital — it's the route to it.

The same pattern one level up: one journey, any service — healthcare, pension, certificates and grievances all sit behind the same "start with what you need" front door.

02 — Booking, without teaching ORS first

Two questions, then a real handoff

Someone without an appointment doesn't need an account or a login to get oriented — just two questions before CarePath explains the government booking flow in plain language and hands off to the real service.

The follow-through matters as much as the explanation: a numbered guide to the official Online Registration System, with an explicit "you are leaving CarePath" notice before the handoff — never a fake booking form pretending to be the real thing.

03 — One next step, live, for the whole visit

From confirmation to "go to Room 204"

This is the core loop: a single journey view that updates in place as the visit progresses, instead of a static confirmation the user has to reinterpret each time.

Four states of one screen, not four screens: appointment confirmed → checked in and waiting → a room change surfaced as a toast the moment it happens → called. The "What changed" log underneath every state exists so a person can trust the current instruction without needing to ask a human to confirm it.
For a visit that's already booked, one lookup — mobile number plus appointment ID — opens straight into the current step, no account needed.

04 — The other half of the loop

Staff side: the same journey, from the desk

The patient's "your turn" isn't magic — it's a staff member at Registration, Doctor, Lab or Pharmacy pressing a real action. Building this side first is what made the patient side honest.

One shared state, four workstations. Marking a patient arrived on this screen is the same event that moves their journey view forward on the patient's phone.

Design system snapshot

Quiet, trustworthy, plain-spoken

Deep teal for anything trustworthy or actionable, soft mint for information at rest, warm off-white underneath everything. Amber is reserved for one job — telling you something just changed.

Deep teal
Actions, trust
Soft mint
Surfaces at rest
Warm off-white
Base canvas
Amber
"Something changed"
Ink
Body text
Go to Room 204.
Fraunces, medium italic — every headline is written as the one sentence that matters right now.
Body and UI copy sit in Inter at a plain, readable size, so the serif headline stays the only voice doing any performing. Cards are rounded and lightly bordered rather than shadowed; every primary action is a full-width teal bar so there's never a guess about what to press next.

Honesty check

What's really working vs. what's simulated

FUNCTIONAL IN THIS PROTOTYPE
  • Every screen shown here is a real, navigable state — no dummy buttons or dead-end cards.
  • Journey step, queue position and room all update from one shared state, live.
  • Staff actions and the patient's view are wired to the same data.
  • Accessibility, read-aloud and language controls are present on every screen.
STILL SYNTHETIC / OUT OF SCOPE
  • ORS is a real external app; CarePath explains it but doesn't submit bookings there.
  • Patients, tokens and hospital data are synthetic demo records.
  • No SMS/USSD/IVR infrastructure — the keypad flow is a concept, not a live channel.
  • Translations are directional and need native-speaker review before real use.

If I kept going

Next steps

P0

Usability-test all four journeys.

To find out whether people actually understand the next action, not just whether I do.
P0

Audit every interactive element again, at scale.

Ten days catches the obvious dead ends, not all of them.
P1

Run real accessibility testing with assistive-tech users.

Keyboard, screen reader and contrast behavior need people, not just checklists.
P1

Prototype the SMS / USSD / IVR path for real.

The keypad idea only proves itself once it works without a smartphone in the loop.
P2

Extend the pattern to pension, certificates and grievances at the same depth as healthcare.

The skeleton is already built to carry them.

Reflection

Not "a nicer government form"

The decision that shaped everything else was to stop competing with the government system and start reducing the uncertainty around it — before, during and after the transaction.

That moves the real question from "does this look better than the official portal" to "can someone understand what they need, prepare correctly, reach the right official service, and know what happens next." The keypad concept pushes that further: a family member or a registration clerk can carry someone through the journey who'd never open the app themselves.

— designed, built and tested over 10 days
